posts.text: Reentrancy lets an attacker slip back into a contract before its state finishes updating.
An external call transfers control to the called contract, which may call back into the original function.
Reentrancy is not limited to Ether transfers; any call to another contract can create a re-entry path.
Mitigate by updating state before external calls and, if needed, adding a reentrancy guard; also examine cross-function paths.
Can you verify that every external interaction in your code follows the checks-effects-interactions order?
Unchecked external call result can silently fail a contract, letting it continue as if the operation succeeded.
Low-level calls return a boolean success flag that the caller can inspect.
The root cause is that the caller does not check the success flag returned by a low-level call.
If a failure is ignored, later logic may depend on an operation that never completed.
Mitigation: always check call outcomes and define explicit failure handling. Review: does the failure path have explicit handling?
Unchecked external call result can silently fail a contract, letting it continue as if the operation succeeded, exposing hidden risk.
Low‑level calls return a boolean success flag that the caller can inspect, providing a way to detect failures.
The root cause is that the caller does not check the success flag returned by a low‑level call.
If the failure flag is ignored, subsequent logic may depend on an operation that never completed, corrupting state.
Mitigation: check call outcomes and define explicit failure handling. Review: does the failure path have explicit handling beyond the success branch?

posts.text: Missing access control lets anyone call privileged functions. A sensitive function without adequate authorization can be called by an unintended account.
The root cause is missing or inconsistently applied permissions across privileged entry points, allowing unintended callers to execute critical logic.
Different privileged operations can require different roles, so a single missing check may expose several functions.
Mitigate by defining roles explicitly and testing unauthorized calls for every privileged operation.
How will you verify that role assignment and revocation themselves are permission-sensitive and correctly restricted?
Missing access control lets an unintended account call privileged functions.
Permissions are missing or applied inconsistently across privileged entry points, creating the gap.
Different privileged operations can require different roles.
Mitigate by defining roles explicitly and testing unauthorized calls for every privileged operation.
How will you verify that role assignment and removal, which are permission-sensitive operations, are correctly restricted?

If your contract trusts a price feed without resistance, a low-liquidity pool can be manipulated and stale data may be used. Have you verified feed liquidity and timestamps? DM to discuss a security review.
Using tx.origin for auth lets a malicious intermediary contract trick a victim into authorizing actions. Have you checked caller-based checks on all call paths? DM to discuss a security review.
Can a loop over growing on-chain data exceed the gas limit? Unbounded iteration can grow work without bound, eventually stalling the contract. DM to discuss a security review.
